Metal radio promotion for independent bands

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 2 min read Genre playbooks

On this page
  • The metal radio map
  • Define the programming fit
  • Prepare the radio assets
  • Choose a pitch angle that belongs to the genre
  • A practical campaign plan
  • Mistakes to avoid

Metal succeeds on radio at the show level. A station that looks broadly alternative may carry one two-hour program where doom, black metal, hardcore, death metal, or progressive releases are selected by a deeply informed host. That specialist—not a generic station inbox—is usually the campaign's real destination.

The metal radio map

College and community metal shows anchor the campaign, with active internet programs, regional heavy-music shows, and selected syndicated programs extending the reach. Commercial active-rock playlists are a later-stage target for the small subset of releases that fit that format.

  • College metal directors and specialty hosts
  • Community heavy-music shows with public playlists
  • Regional programs tied to venues and scenes
  • Presenter-led internet radio and podcasts that publish tracklists
  • Syndicated metal shows with transparent submission routes

Define the programming fit

Use the actual subgenre and inspect the host's recent range. A traditional-heavy-metal show and an extreme-metal program are not interchangeable even if both pages say metal.

Use recent playlists rather than a station's decade-old format description. Write down two or three comparable artists the show actually aired, the program name, and the contact responsible. Those notes become both your qualification record and the first sentence of a human pitch.

Prepare the radio assets

  • A focus track chosen for the target show's lane
  • A broadcast-safe edit if lyrics or samples require it
  • Accurate band, label, territory, release, and track metadata
  • One-sheet with subgenre, comparable artists, and notable tour dates
  • Artwork and photos that can be published with proper credits

Place everything behind one stable link. The first email should remain light: no large attachments and no maze of social profiles. A programmer should be able to hear the track in one click and find a download only if they want it.

Choose a pitch angle that belongs to the genre

Demonstrate scene literacy without writing a review of your own record. Name the exact subgenre, one recent playlist fit, relevant personnel or label facts, and a confirmed date in the market when available.

Claims such as “next big artist” are unusable. Replace them with specific evidence: a sold-out local date, a named producer, support from a relevant show, a chart week, or a genuine connection to the market. If there is no evidence yet, a precise description of the song is enough.

A practical campaign plan

  1. Build a first wave of twenty shows where the subgenre match is obvious.
  2. Send two to three weeks before release, unless a station specifies another window.
  3. Follow up once after seven to ten days and stop if there is no response.
  4. Check public playlists and chart reports; thank confirmed supporters.
  5. Use real results to qualify a second wave, then preserve the relationships for the next release.

Separate premieres, interviews, single spins, recurring rotation, and playlist or chart appearances. Screenshots are useful records, but retain a public URL or direct confirmation whenever possible.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Calling a broad format match “research” without checking the actual show
  • Sending the wrong version, missing metadata, or an expiring private link
  • Pitching multiple unrelated tracks in one first email
  • Automating repeated follow-ups or ignoring a station's submission policy
  • Paying anyone who promises undisclosed or guaranteed airplay

Frequently asked questions

What radio stations play independent metal?

College metal directors, community specialty programs, regional heavy-music shows, active internet programs, and selected syndicated shows are the practical first targets.

What should I send with a metal radio pitch?

Send one focus track, a stream/download route, clear subgenre, release date, full metadata, and a clean edit if required. Include tour dates only when they are confirmed and relevant to the market.

How many stations should a first campaign target?

Begin with 40 to 80 genuinely matched stations or shows, not every station that uses a broad genre label. Send in waves so playlist and response data can improve the next group.
